title: Ossobuco alla Milanese
subtitle: Braised veal shin with gremolata, served with risotto alla Milanese
excerpt: Ossobuco alla milanese is a Milanese classic: thick cross-cut veal shin pieces braised in white wine, stock, and vegetables until falling-off-the-bone tender. It is finished with gremolata -- a mixture of lemon zest, garlic, and parsley -- stirred in at the table. It is traditionally served with risotto alla Milanese.
sourceNotes: Ossobuco alla milanese is one of the defining dishes of Milanese cooking, documented since the nineteenth century. The word means hollow bone, referring to the marrow-filled shin cross-section. The gremolata (lemon zest, garlic, parsley) is added at the table, not cooked. The dish is traditionally served with risotto alla Milanese (saffron risotto).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the braised ossobuco in its sauce. Reheat gently. Make fresh gremolata when serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves if made a day ahead. Make fresh gremolata when serving.

content.text: Ossobuco needs a braising vessel wide enough to hold the veal shin pieces in a single layer. The pieces must be tied with kitchen string around their circumference before braising to stop the meat falling off the bone as it cooks. The gremolata is a raw condiment added at the table -- it is not cooked into the sauce.

items.prepNote: 4 thick cross-cut shin pieces, each about 300g and 4cm thick, tied with kitchen string

content.text: Season {{veal-shoulder}} veal shin pieces and dust lightly in {{plain-flour}} flour. Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil and {{unsalted-butter}} butter in a wide heavy pan over medium-high heat. Brown the veal on both sides, about 5 minutes per side, working in batches. Remove.

Reduce heat to medium. Add {{onion}} onion, {{celery}} celery, and {{carrot}} carrot to the pan and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{garlic}} garlic and cook for 1 minute. Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} wine and simmer until reduced by half.

Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} tomatoes, hot {{chicken-stock}} stock, {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves, and {{salt-table}} salt. Return the veal shin pieces standing upright in the pan. Bring to a simmer, cover tightly, and cook at the lowest possible heat for 1 hour 30 minutes until the meat is very tender and beginning to fall from the bone. Check every 30 minutes and add a splash of water if the liquid reduces too much.

Mix {{lemon}} lemon zest, grated {{garlic}} garlic, and {{parsley-flat}} parsley together for the gremolata. Remove the string from the ossobuco. Serve with risotto alla Milanese or mashed potato, with the gremolata scattered over at the table.

items.symptom: The meat fell off the bone during braising
items.cause: The shin pieces were not tied with string before cooking.
items.fix: Always tie a length of kitchen string around the circumference of each veal shin piece before braising. This holds the meat on the bone while it cooks. The string is removed at serving.

content.text: Ossobuco alla milanese is the most prestigious meat dish of Milan. It is the Sunday braise, the dinner-party centrepiece, and the dish that defines Milanese hospitality. The bone marrow inside the hollow shin is considered a delicacy -- a small spoon is traditionally provided to scoop it out. The correct accompaniment is risotto alla Milanese, the saffron risotto, which soaks up the rich braising juices.
